teach.title: An action with nobody attached
teach.say: *Cantat* tells you who and when: she sings, now. Strip both away and you have **the infinitive (the 'to' form)**, *modus īnfīnītīvus*: *cantāre*, to sing — the action named, with no person and no time. On its own it says nothing; it leans on another verb, and Latin's are *potest* (can), *vult* (wants), *audet* (dares) and *necesse est* (it is necessary).

teach.title: Add -re to the stem vowel
teach.say: Most verbs simply put **-re** after the vowel their stem already ends in. That gives **-āre** for verbs like *cantat* (*cantāre*, *natāre*, *portāre*), **-ēre** for verbs like *videt* (*vidēre*, *tacēre*, *habēre*), and **-īre** for verbs like *audit* (*audīre*, *dormīre*, *venīre*). The dictionary prints this form second, right after the *I* form.

teach.title: The third family: -ere, with a short e
teach.say: One family has no long vowel of its own, so it slips a short *e* in before the -re: *legit* → **legere**, *ascendit* → **ascendere**, *facit* → **facere**, *vēndit* → **vēndere**. It is worth hearing the difference: *vidēre* has a long ē and *legere* a short one, and only the long ē belongs to the family of *videt*.

teach.title: To be done: -rī, or a bare -ī
teach.say: For the passive (the 'is done' form) the -e of the ending turns into a long ī: *cantārī* (to be sung), *vidērī* (to be seen), *audīrī* (to be heard). The third family, which had no vowel to begin with, drops the r as well and keeps only **-ī**: *legī* (to be read), *capī* (to be caught). *Avis ā puerō capī potest* = the bird can be caught by the boy.

teach.title: The handful that double a consonant
teach.say: A few very common verbs never took a stem vowel, so they double a consonant instead of adding -re: *est* → **esse** (to be), *potest* → **posse** (to be able), *vult* → **velle** (to want), *fert* → **ferre** (to carry). *Īre* (to go) is the odd one the other way, a stem so short that only -re is left. Learn these five by heart; two or three more of the same kind turn up much later.

teach.title: The 'to' form, or the verb itself?
teach.say: Two near-misses catch beginners. *Currere* (to run) beside *currunt* (they are running): the infinitive has -re and leans on *volunt*, the finite verb has a person's ending and stands alone. And *tacēre* (to be quiet) beside *tacē!* (be quiet!): the command is short, stands by itself and usually has a name beside it. If a *potest*, *vult* or *audet* is anywhere near, the -re form is an infinitive.

core.text: Latin's 'to' form is **the infinitive (the 'to' form)**, *modus īnfīnītīvus*: *volāre* = to fly, *vidēre* = to see, *pōnere* = to put, *audīre* = to hear. It ends in -re in the active and -rī (3rd conjugation just -ī) in the passive (the 'is done' form): *vidērī* = to be seen, *pōnī* = to be put. It hangs on *potest* (can), *vult* (wants), *audet* (dares), *dēbet* (ought) and *necesse est* (it is necessary).
*To fly*, *to be seen*: the plain verb with *to*, or without it after *can* and *must*. It names the action without saying who or when.
Active: stem + -re (-āre, -ēre, -ere, -īre). Passive: -ārī, -ērī, -ī, -īrī. Irregular: *esse* (to be), *posse* (to be able), *velle* (to want), *ferre* (to carry), *īre* (to go).

invented.la: Puella cantāre vult, sed nōn potest.
invented.en: The girl wants to sing but cannot.
The slaves have to carry the master.

core.text: In the 2nd conjugation the infinitive and the command look alike: *vidēre* (to see) beside *vidē!* (look!); in the 3rd, *pōnere* beside *pōne!*. The infinitive always ends in -re or -rī and leans on a verb like *potest* or *vult*; the command stands on its own, often with a name and an exclamation mark.

more.text: From the learner's notes: the infinitive has no person and no number; it is a mood, like the indicative and the imperative, that works as a noun in the sentence (the object of *want*, *can*, *dare*, *ought*) yet can still take its own object. The active ending is -(e)re, the e dropping after a vowel stem but staying in weak i-stems (*percutere*, not *percutire*); the passive -(r)ī drops its r in consonant and (i)-stems (*frangī*, *percutī*). *Esse*, *posse*, *velle*, *ferre* double a consonant instead of using a variable vowel; only *ferre* has a passive, *ferrī*.

Ørberg cap. X: -re / -rī; *necesse est* + infinitive; *vult*, *potest*, *audet*. The infinitive with an accusative as its own subject — *Quīntum vīvum esse vident* (they see that Quintus is alive, r10:122.1) — is the next skill, the accusative and infinitive. Perfect (*vēnisse*) and future (*ventūrum esse*) infinitives come later. A&G §451–456.
